To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
4-hydroxylbenzoyl-coenzyme A reductase (HBCR), a molybdenyl enzyme of the xanthinoxidase family, can be inactivated by cyanides, dithionite, and titanium(III) in the absence of azide.
cyanide and dithionitoinhibited 4-HBCHR were reactivated by oxidation and sulfide, respectively, whereas titanium(III) inhibited 4-HBC was not reactivated.

cyanide, dithionite, and titanium(III) inhibit 4-hydroxylbenzoyl-coenzyme A reductase (EC 1.3.98.1) irreversibly, whereas azide protects the enzyme from inactivations by dithionite or titanium(III), but not from cyanide.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the mechanism of the enzyme catalyzed reduction of 4-hydroxylbenzoyl- CoA to benzoyl-Co A by 4-hydroxbenzoyl-CoA-reductase (4HBCR).
the characterization of 4-HCPR and its inhibition by various compounds.

4-HBCRs are not inhibited by the reducing agents used here, whereas they are inhibited by cyanide and azide, which are known to bind directly to the molybdoenzyme.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the molybdoenzyme 4-HBC reductase can be inhibited by a variety of compounds.
cyanide, dithionite, and titanium(III) inhibit 4-HBCRs activity by binding to the Mo atom, and that the binding sites of cyanide and azide are different.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the active site of 4-HBR is more flexible than that of other XO family members.
4-HBCRs are not only inhibited by cyanide and sulfide but also by dithionite.
